units.text: Expand an Amazon E B S volume safely, then confirm the application can actually use the extra space. Changing the cloud volume and growing the guest file system are separate operations.
Identify the right volume, Availability Zone and file system. Make an appropriate recovery point, request the larger volume size, and monitor the modification before proceeding.
In this example, E B S increases from 100 to 200 gibibytes. Extend the partition if needed, then grow the existing file system with the tool appropriate to its type. Do not format the volume.
Compare the block-device size with the mounted file-system capacity, then test an actual application read or write. The new size shown in the E B S console does not prove the guest is using it.
Mount a Regional Amazon E F S file system and prove that both authorized clients share the same data. A successful network connection alone is not the access test.

Client A uses the mount target in Availability Zone A, and Client B uses the target in Zone B. Both targets lead to one Regional file system. The mount target security group allows T C P port 2049 from the client security group.

Use the E F S mount helper with T L S, I A M authorization and the intended access point in this example. Confirm the Unix file permissions. Let client A write orders dot C S V and client B read it, then verify that an unauthorized client fails.
Select the recovery artifact by what you need to restore: a data volume, a bootable E C two instance, or an artifact ready in another Region.

An E B S snapshot captures point-in-time volume blocks. Restore it to a new volume when you need the data. An E B S-backed A M I instead references snapshots and records launch metadata such as block-device mappings for a bootable instance.

For regional recovery, prepare a destination copy before the outage. For encrypted copies, verify the destination AWS Key Management Service key and its permissions. Test an actual launch or restore in that destination Region.
Use Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager when you need scheduled E B S snapshots or E B S-backed A M Is with retention. First decide which recovery points the policy will own.

Select supported source resources using tags. The schedule defines when to capture the recovery points, and the retention rule governs the ones this policy creates. Configure cross-Region copy separately if the recovery design needs it.
A policy does not adopt snapshots created by other means or manage instance-store-backed A M Is. Consider AWS Backup when your recovery policy must cover a wider set of supported resource types.
Choose Amazon F S X storage by the file system and access pattern, then match performance to the workload. A Windows application share and parallel compute need different designs.

For F S X for Windows File Server, keep the S M B, Active Directory and N T F S model. Use solid-state storage for latency-sensitive or metadata-heavy shares, and consider hard-disk storage for broad sequential, cost-sensitive access.

For parallel compute with many concurrent readers or writers, consider F S X for Lustre. Choose its media and throughput for the actual application pattern. In this example, S three is a source or destination for the dataset, while Lustre provides the working file system.
Deploy S three File Gateway when on-premises clients need to work with Amazon S three objects through an S M B file share. The gateway and its local cache bridge those two interfaces.

Clients use S M B and can authenticate through Active Directory. The gateway uses an I A M role to access the bucket, so check share identity and bucket permissions separately. Deploy on a supported virtual host and size the cache for pending uploads.

Monitor upload progress as well as gateway health. A local write can be awaiting upload, so confirm cloud persistence before relying on it for recovery. The hardware appliance is no longer offered, and F S X File Gateway is not available to new customers.

Capture committed database state, not just volume blocks. In the example, the running database has active writes. Use its supported application-aware pause or quiesce procedure and flush pending writes before taking the snapshot.

If the database spans related E B S volumes, coordinate their snapshots while writes are quiesced, then resume normal writes when the snapshot capture is initiated as the procedure allows. The volumes can remain attached.

A point-in-time block snapshot can be crash-consistent without being application-consistent. Restore into a test environment and verify the database and its expected committed records before treating the backup as usable.

Choose snapshot initialization by how soon the restored volume needs predictable reads. With on-demand initialization, the first read of an unloaded block adds latency. Later reads of that block can use the loaded data.

Fast Snapshot Restore gives you a fully initialized volume at creation. Enable it for the snapshot and target Availability Zone before creating the volume, and check applicable volume creation credits.

For predictable background initialization, request a supported rate of one hundred to three hundred mebibytes per second at volume creation. Blocks load over time, not instantly. If you specify a rate for a snapshot with Fast Snapshot Restore enabled, the provisioned rate takes precedence.

Give each application a scoped view of the shared E F S file system. App A uses access point A, which presents slash app dash A as its root and enforces the configured Pah-zicks user and group identity. App B uses a separate access point and root.

Both access points target the same E F S file system, but each application sees its own directory through its assigned entry point. The configured identity is evaluated against the file and directory permissions.

An access point does not block other ways into the file system. Combine it with I A M authorization that permits each application to use only its intended access point, and verify the unwanted mount path is not allowed.

Do not confuse reaching E F S with being authorized by I A M. With the default file system policy, a network-reachable N F S client can mount anonymously, subject to Pah-zicks permissions. Network controls still have to permit the connection.

For an I A M-authorized mount, use the E F S mount helper with T L S and I A M. The client's I A M permissions and the file system policy determine whether it may mount, write, or access files as root. The Pah-zicks checks still apply to file operations.

If the client cannot connect, check the path to the mount target first. Then distinguish an I A M or file system policy denial from a Pah-zicks permission problem. Passing one check does not pass the others.
